title: The Kerosene Lamp
medium: Charcoal, with red Conté and colored crayons, touches of graphite, and scraping, heightened with white oil paint, on canvas prepared with a glue ground
altText: A drawing on canvas made with charcoal, red and colored crayons, graphite and white oil paint. Its playful marks and shapes are said by the museum to suggest ideas, and the work is often read as a view of the artist's studio.

source.verifiedBy: Art Institute of Chicago API record: title, artist (Joan Miró, Spanish, 1893-1983), date, medium, place of origin, credit line, curatorial description summary (Miró as a leading Surrealist; often read as a depiction of his studio; elements suggest ideas rather than fixed meanings) and public-domain flag (false) read from the record. context: Made in 1924 by the Spanish artist Joan Miró, a leading Surrealist. The museum record lists charcoal, red Conté and colored crayons, graphite and scraping, heightened with white oil paint, on canvas, and says the drawing is often read as a depiction of his studio, with elements meant to suggest ideas rather than carry fixed meanings.

descriptions.k: This is a drawing with crayon, charcoal, and a little white paint. The title is The Kerosene Lamp. Many people think it shows the artist's studio. What simple shapes can you find? What do they remind you of?
descriptions.g12: Joan Miró made this drawing with charcoal, red and colored crayons, and white paint. The title is The Kerosene Lamp, and people often think it shows his art studio. His shapes are playful and simple. They are meant to give you ideas. What idea does each mark give you?
descriptions.g35: Joan Miró, a Spanish artist, made The Kerosene Lamp in 1924 using charcoal, crayons, graphite, and white oil paint on canvas. The museum says it is often read as his studio, but the shapes are meant to suggest ideas instead of showing exact things. What ideas do the marks give you? How do they feel like a room or a dream?
descriptions.g68: Miró made The Kerosene Lamp in 1924, combining charcoal, red Conté and colored crayons, graphite, scraping, and white oil paint on canvas. The museum says it is often read as a depiction of his studio, with elements meant to suggest ideas rather than fixed meanings. How does a drawing like this invite you to read marks as symbols, and what is the difference between a sign and a picture?
descriptions.g910: In The Kerosene Lamp (1924), Miró draws with charcoal, crayon, graphite, and scraped surfaces heightened with white paint. The museum notes it is often read as his studio, yet its elements are meant to suggest ideas rather than carry fixed meanings. As a leading Surrealist, Miró invites open association. Consider how a title anchors the drawing while leaving room for personal interpretation, and how materials affect its look.
descriptions.g1112: Miró's The Kerosene Lamp (1924) belongs to the years when he developed a personal vocabulary of signs. Its mixed drawing media on prepared canvas suggest a studio interior, yet the museum emphasizes that its elements evoke ideas rather than fixed meanings. How does the work balance reference and indeterminacy, and what does it mean for a title like 'Kerosene Lamp' to orient but not explain an image?

teacherNote.context: A 1924 mixed-media drawing on canvas by Joan Miró in the Art Institute of Chicago. The museum says it is often read as his studio, with elements that suggest ideas rather than fixed meanings. A person must review the image. The work is in copyright, so no image is linked yet.
directions: Have students draw their room using only symbols and simple shapes, then trade and interpret.
Ask students to invent three titles for the drawing and discuss how each changes the view.
Discuss the difference between a picture of an object and a sign for an idea.
